transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-08-12 15:30 UTC
- Duration: 53 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (AuroraEdge Head of ML), Samuel Ortiz (Platform Eng), Laila Ahmed (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
AuroraEdge is exploring reserved capacity (dedicated GPU pools) for latency sensitive inference across their edge-to-cloud product. They have strict isolation and encryption needs; they want a burst policy that avoids noisy neighbor impact. Discussed fallbacks to hosted API for overflow, on-prem/private options, and key management. Next steps agreed: send pricing + SLA, schedule infra deep dive, share traffic samples.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm maya from redwood, joining with diego from our se team. how's afternoon, priya?
[00:06] Priya Nair: good, thanks. we've got sam and laila on too. i'll hand it to sam for a quick infra snapshot.
[00:12] Samuel Ortiz: yeah hi all. auroraedge runs a mix of GKE in region-us-west and some colo racks for very low-latency inference. currently we use a mixture of hosted endpoints and an internal model server for experiments. we're looking to move to a dedicated reservation to guarantee latency under 60ms p95 for our public inference path.
[00:30] Die go (SE): sorry, diego here. p95 60ms, ok, is that for short responses or long streams?
[00:36] Samuel Ortiz: mostly short responses, average token length 40-60, some longer chat sessions but the mission-critical flows are sub-200 tokens.
[00:45] Priya Nair: just to add, throughput spikes from campaigns can go up 6x for 10-20 minutes. so we'll need a burst plan.
[00:53] Maya Chen: great context. one thing we usually discuss is isolation: do you need physical tenant isolation (fully dedicated nodes) or logical isolation (multi-tenant with strict namespaces)?
[01:02] Laila Ahmed: security is a blocker. for any PII flows we need tenant separation and customer-managed keys — HSM-backed KMS preferred. soc two plus, plus audit trail for every inference. so physical isolation is preferred, but we want to understand cost delta.
[01:18] Diego Ruiz: totally. Redwood Dedicated supports both: fully segregated GPU pools (physical) or tenant-aware scheduling. physical gives you strong isolation and dedicated resource guarantees; logical is cheaper but you trade off potential noisy neighbor risk. for KMS we integrate with customer KMS/HSM via key import or dedicated key proxy, and we can capture per-request audit entries.
[01:40] Samuel Ortiz: quick question — if we do dedicated but spike above reserved capacity, what's the overflow story? we don't want dropped requests.
[01:48] Maya Chen: good call. two common patterns: one is burst capacity from reserved pool within the same region (we can provision burst instances as part of the contract, but they are limited). second is overflow routing to our hosted endpoints as a fallback — that preserves availability but you must accept possible differences in data residency and slightly different SLAs.
[02:07] Priya Nair: the hosted fallback raises data residency flags for us. some customers require all inference to be in-region for legal reasons. can we route to another dedicated pool in a different region?
[02:17] Diego Ruiz: yes, we can route to a dedicated pool in another region assuming contract covers that capacity. there's also warm-standby pools you can keep reserved at lower compute configs for quick spin-up. there's tradeoffs between cost and failover speed.
[02:32] Laila Ahmed: audit logs — we need 12 months retention, immutable logs, and SSO/S A M L integration with our IdP. is that supported?
[02:40] Maya Chen: Redwood supports SSO/SAML (we might have spelled it out funny in places), role-based access, and we can retain audit logs for the required period under enterprise add-on. We'll send the compliance appendix.
[02:52] Samuel Ortiz: can you walk through how you handle KV cache and pre-warming? caches are big for our workloads.
[02:58] Diego Ruiz: sure. we have prefix and KV cache strategies. for models with long contexts we keep KV cached in GPU memory during session duration. for pre-warming, we support pre-baked warmers that run the model on representative prompts to populate the KV and kernel paths. that reduces first-token latency for new instances. we also do continuous micro-batching to keep throughput efficient without exploding latency.
[03:20] Priya Nair: curious about quantization — would that affect accuracy for our NLU metrics? we have critical intent classification.
[03:26] Diego Ruiz: quantization options are model-dependent; we provide recommended quantization profiles per model and run evals against your prompt set to estimate quality drop. usually lower-bit quantization yields modest throughput gains with small quality regressions; we can include a recommended profile in the bench spreadsheet.
[03:40] Maya Chen: on pricing and commitment, reserved pools are monthly or annual. you commit to a certain number of GPU slots (or GPU hours) and that guarantees throughput. we also have burst credits that can be purchased or applied as part of the contract.
[03:52] Samuel Ortiz: what about autoscale? can we auto-scale beyond reserved with preemption? we worry about noisy tenants if someone else bursts.
[04:00] Diego Ruiz: autoscale can be configured, but preemption on Dedicated pools is a policy choice. With fully dedicated pools there's no other tenant on those GPUs, so preemption is less of a concern. If you use shared dedicated (reserved capacity that still co-locates low-priority workloads) we can enforce tenant scheduling policies and guardrails.
[04:18] Laila Ahmed: network isolation — we need VPC peering and private endpoints, ideally no public egress. do you support VPC-based private deployment paths?
[04:26] Maya Chen: yes — Redwood Private or VPC options allow private control plane and private endpoints. for some customers we deploy a private control plane into their VPC. There is an on-prem packaging option for air-gapped setups.
[04:38] Priya Nair: timeline-wise, if we like the proposal, we'd want to pilot in Q4 and go GA early Q1. budget cycle closes late Q3. is that feasible?
[04:47] Maya Chen: absolutely reasonable. typical pilot timeline is 4-6 weeks: initial provisioning, benchmark runs, and a pilot SLA.
[04:53] Samuel Ortiz: benchmarks — what data do you need from us?
[04:56] Diego Ruiz: sample payloads, token distributions, sample traffic trace ideally 1 hour of representative traffic with timestamps, and critical prompt sets. we'll use those to run throughput and p95 latency sims and produce cost estimates.
[05:09] Priya Nair: ok we'll assemble that. also, who would be our CSM?
[05:12] Maya Chen: after contract, you'll get a dedicated CSM and an assigned solutions engineer — usually diego or a colleague for the initial ramp.
[05:20] Laila Ahmed: last security question — how do you manage keys during model inference? does the model ever see raw keys or do you do envelope encryption?
[05:26] Diego Ruiz: envelope encryption is our standard: customer KMS keys encrypt dataset keys; we never bake raw customer master keys into the runtime. For HSM integrations we can set up key proxies so keys never leave customer control.
[05:38] Priya Nair: if we do a hybrid approach — Dedicated for PII flows and Hosted for non-PII — will the developer experience differ significantly? we want a single SDK if possible.
[05:47] Maya Chen: SDKs and APIs are consistent across Hosted/Dedicated/Private. you can pin model versions and routing policies in config. observability might differ in retention windows (enterprise add-on), but the developer surface is the same.
[06:00] Samuel Ortiz: any concerns about kernel selection and performance variability across A100 vs H100?
[06:06] Diego Ruiz: we profile per GPU and automatically select kernels; performance varies — H100 gives better throughput on larger sequence lengths. we’ll include model/hardware pairing recommendations in the bench.
[06:20] Priya Nair: pricing sensitivity — we have a hard budget for infra. would you provide guidance on cheapest configuration that still meets 60ms p95?
[06:28] Maya Chen: yes we'll run cost/perf tradeoff profiles: fewer higher-end GPUs vs more lower-end GPUs, batching windows, quantization, and caching. Diego will put together a cost sensitivity table.
[06:40] Samuel Ortiz: one more — observability: token-level cost and latency breakdowns are important for our finance team.
[06:46] Maya Chen: Redwood Console includes per-token cost, per-route and per-model latency breakdowns; we can enable token accounting for your routes.
[06:54] Priya Nair: great. i think that's it from our side.
[06:57] Maya Chen: ok quick recap: we'll send pricing + SLA appendix, diego will run preliminary throughput and cost estimates after you send payloads and traces, and we'll schedule a 60-90 minute infra deep dive to discuss VPC, KMS, and deployment topology. any other open items?
[07:15] Laila Ahmed: we'll confirm data residency constraints in the doc we send.
[07:18] Samuel Ortiz: timeline — we'll aim to get assets to you by next friday.
[07:22] Maya Chen: perfect. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and artifacts.

End of meeting.
